The central question is whether a communication protocol that emerges among a population of agents can survive the replacement of individual agents with newly-initialized ones — and if so, under what conditions it remains functional rather than drifting or collapsing. The key concepts are: emergent signaling (agents develop symbol-meaning mappings through interaction rather than design), compositional vs. holistic protocols (whether meanings are built from parts or are atomic), and population-level equilibrium (the protocol as a Nash equilibrium that new agents either converge to or destabilize). The turnover problem is specifically about whether a protocol acts as an attractor in the learning landscape — can a naive agent, trained against incumbents who already speak the protocol, be pulled into fluency, or does it instead corrupt the incumbents through gradient updates?

What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the asymmetry between comprehension and production: a new agent can often learn to decode an existing protocol before it can generate it reliably, and if the training setup updates incumbents based on interactions with the newcomer, even partial production errors by the newcomer can erode the protocol's precision among agents who had previously stabilized — a kind of fluency contamination that aggregate metrics like task reward completely obscure. Experts also worry about protocol degeneracy under turnover: two locally stable but mutually incompatible dialects can coexist in a mixed population, and turnover rate determines which one wins or whether the population fragments, a dynamic that looks fine in per-episode reward curves until it catastrophically doesn't.

Freezing incumbents during onboarding buys you experimental isolability: you can cleanly measure whether a protocol is learnable by a naive agent as a fixed target, separating "is the protocol stable as a basin of attraction" from "do incumbents adapt to accommodate the newcomer." This is what Mordatch & Abbeel (2018) effectively assumed in their Grounded Communication environments — the emergent language was evaluated against frozen or near-frozen partners, which is why their compositionality results are cleaner than most follow-up work that allows co-adaptation. It also gives you a reproducible onboarding curriculum: the target distribution doesn't shift under the learner, so you can actually measure sample efficiency and convergence, which matters when comparing protocol robustness across architectures.

What you silently give up is bidirectional plasticity — the empirically documented property that in real human language communities, and in open-ended agent systems like those studied by Lowe et al. and the OpenAI hide-and-seek work, incumbents continuously adjust register, compression, and reference strategies in response to a naive interlocutor. In human psycholinguistics this is called partner-specific lexical entrainment, and it's not cosmetic: Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs (1986) showed referential efficiency improving 40–50% over repeated interaction specifically because both parties adapted. When you freeze incumbents you eliminate the possibility that the protocol itself is the wrong unit of analysis — that what's actually stable in robust systems isn't a fixed codebook but a co-adaptation dynamic, and a newcomer doesn't need to learn the protocol so much as learn how to participate in that ongoing negotiation.

If stability is a dynamic rather than a codebook, drift can't be defined as deviation from a reference symbol table — it has to be defined functionally, as degradation in the mutual predictability of agent behavior given signals, measured across interaction pairs rather than against a ground truth. The cleanest operationalization is something like topographic similarity (how well the metric structure of the signal space mirrors the metric structure of the meaning space, per Brighten & Kirby 2001 and later automated by Lazaridou et al. 2018), but this only catches compositional drift; holistic protocols can drift invisibly under topographic metrics while task reward stays high because agents overfit to a shared but increasingly idiosyncratic codebook that excludes newcomers. A more diagnostic measure is generalization gap under partner substitution — hold out a fraction of agents, run protocol-trained agents against novel partners, and measure reward drop; Jaques et al. (2019) in Social Influence used influence-based rewards that implicitly tracked something like this, finding that agents with higher causal influence on partners generalized better, which suggests influence structure is a more stable invariant than symbol identity.

The distinguishability problem is genuinely hard in finite windows: drift and evolution are the same trajectory, differentiated only by whether downstream functionality is preserved — which you can't know until you test against a distribution of future interaction partners you don't yet have. One partial solution is causal probing at multiple time horizons: if the mapping from referent to signal is becoming more agent-pair-specific over time (measurable by training a decoder on signals from one pair and testing on another), that's drift even if task reward is flat; if the mapping is becoming more compressed and systematic, that's evidence of evolution. The irreducible problem is that a protocol can be simultaneously drifting for excluded agents and evolving for included ones — the population boundary is doing the work, and any single observation window is implicitly conditioned on a particular population slice.

This doesn't use the seed agents as ground truth for correctness but as a coordinate system — drift is defined as the rate of change of that divergence, not its absolute value, so you're measuring velocity rather than position and sidestepping the implicit claim that seed behavior was correct. The minimal structural property is combinatorial expressivity exhaustion: the anchor task must require agents to communicate about a referent space large enough that no compressed, holistic codebook can cover it — forcing the protocol to be generative rather than lookup-based. Concretely, if the referent space has N distinguishable objects and the signal vocabulary has K symbols with length L, you need N > K^L to be unsatisfiable by memorization, which is the design principle behind the large-scale referential games in Choi et al. (2018) and the ShapeWorld environments — but even those were gamed when agents found clustered shortcuts in the perceptual space rather than the symbolic space. The deeper requirement is that the anchor task must have compositional entanglement: performance on unseen referent combinations must be derivable only from correct decomposition of seen ones, not from interpolation in a continuous embedding — which means the task geometry must be discrete and the held-out set must be structured as an out-of-support combinatorial split, not a random holdout.

Even combinatorial exhaustion isn't sufficient if the agent controls its own feature representation, because it can learn a private continuous embedding that technically spans the referent space while being opaque to novel partners — a failure mode Kottur et al. (2017) demonstrated explicitly, showing that agents with higher-capacity perception modules developed less interpretable and less transferable protocols despite perfect task performance. The truly minimal sufficient property is therefore what you might call partner-asymmetric evaluability: the anchor task must be solvable by a receiver that is strictly more constrained than the sender — for instance, a receiver whose architecture cannot learn arbitrary nonlinear decodings — so that the communication channel itself, not a compensating decoder, must carry the information structure. This is related to the information-bottleneck framing but stricter: it's not about compressing the channel, it's about ensuring the receiver's inductive bias forces the sender to externalize structure that would otherwise stay implicit, making protocol degradation directly visible in task failure rather than hidden in representational slack.

A specific and underappreciated fact is that protocol stability under turnover is non-monotonic in population size: small populations collapse under turnover because each agent's idiosyncratic usage has high weight in the shared signal distribution, but very large populations also degrade because the protocol becomes a lowest-common-denominator pidgin that compresses out the precise distinctions newcomers never had incentive to learn. The sweet spot — where turnover is most survivable — appears at intermediate population sizes where there is enough redundancy to absorb individual drift but enough selection pressure to maintain expressivity. Liptak et al. and related iterated learning simulations suggest this non-monotonicity is real and that the critical population threshold scales roughly with the protocol's minimum description length: more expressive protocols require larger minimum viable populations to survive equivalent turnover rates, which means a protocol that evolved under large-population conditions can be catastrophically fragile when deployed in a smaller operational cluster even if it was perfectly stable at training scale.

The practical implication that experts miss is that scaling up agent count during training is not conservative with respect to turnover robustness — it can actively create protocols that are brittle at deployment scale, because the training population was large enough to maintain protocol complexity that the deployment population cannot sustain. This is an inversion of the usual assumption that more training resources produce more robust systems, and it has no analog in single-agent RL where more training is unambiguously better. It suggests that protocol robustness evaluations should always be conducted at the minimum intended deployment population size, not at training scale, a practice that is almost never followed in published multi-agent communication benchmarks.

Explicit description length minimization has been implemented — the closest direct instantiation is the Minimum Description Length (MDL) regularizer applied to emergent communication by Korbak et al. (2019) and related work using channel capacity penalties in the information bottleneck framing, where a KL term penalizes the mutual information between messages and meanings beyond what task performance requires. The empirical result is not degenerate collapse but something subtler: agents learn maximally compressed protocols that are compositional at the level of the task's natural feature decomposition — they discover the task's intrinsic dimensionality and allocate exactly one signal degree of freedom per task-relevant dimension, which looks like elegant systematicity but is actually fragile in a specific way. The protocol becomes brittle to any referent distribution shift that reveals dimensions the task didn't require distinguishing — newcomers who encounter edge cases outside the training distribution find the protocol has no vocabulary for the distinctions they need, not because the code collapsed but because it was carved precisely to the training manifold.

The turnover-robustness outcome is therefore conditionally positive: MDL-regularized protocols survive turnover better than unregularized ones within the training distribution because shorter codes are easier to acquire with limited interaction budgets, which is exactly what Chaabouni et al. (2020) found when measuring human learnability of agent-generated codes — more compressed codes were acquired faster. But the same compression that aids onboarding destroys robustness to distributional novelty, creating a stability-expressivity-robustness trilemma: you can optimize any two but the third degrades. The practically non-obvious implication is that the right regularization target isn't minimum description length but minimum description length conditional on a held-out referent distribution that includes out-of-support combinations — penalizing complexity only for in-distribution meanings while preserving generative capacity, a target that has no clean closed-form penalty and requires something closer to meta-learning over referent distributions than a fixed KL term.
